chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 6 of 21), sung in pairs that share a meter and a closing line: the poet fears the hour when Death's noose falls and kin carry the body to the fire, sees the body from womb to decay, renounces house, kin and wealth as passing, and confesses his bondage to women; the praise turns on the freeing of the imprisoned gods, Siva's dance in the burning ground, and Murugan as teacher of Siva and of Tamil to Agastya.
structure_note: Paired songs share a meter and a refrain: 1068-1069 (the gods freed from prison), 1070-1071 (the plea to sing Murugan's love for Valli, ending 'praised by the three worlds'), 1072-1073 (red feet and anklets), 1078-1079 (Siva dancing in the burning ground, Murugan the companion of the hunters' parrot), 1080-1081. 1074 is mostly praise of Siva's attributes; 1075 is an akam plea for a lovesick girl.

1067.reading: Before his children, father and wife crowd round wailing, before Death with his cruel eyes casts the noose from his strong hand to bind him, the mind fails and life goes, the poet asks Murugan to give his red-gold feet as a pillar to lean on and show grace. The praise names him bridegroom of the girl of the cool hill where monkeys leap, the warrior who fights the crowding asuras as the gods praise, and the ever-young lord who embraces with love women with moon-like foreheads.
1067.nuance: தம்பம் உனது செம்பொன் அடிகள்: the feet as a pillar (ஸ்தம்பம்) to hold when the body is shaken. The closing epithet, the ever-young lord who embraces women for their delight, turns the language of the poet's own confession into praise of the god's love.

1068.reading: The poet traces the body from its birth in one mother's womb, a shape of legs and arms clothed in skin over oozing flesh and blood, wandering full of illusion, to the wheezing and pitiable old age that ends in death, and asks that before then he be given the life of saying 'Muruga' with love in his heart. The praise tells how the demons laid waste the gem-rich golden city of the king of the gods who rides the rutting elephant, set it on fire, and carried the gods off to prison, and how Murugan set them free.
1068.nuance: The whole remedy is a name: முருகா எனச் சொல் பகர் வாழ்வு, a life of saying 'Muruga'. The city is Indra's Amaravati and the elephant his Airavata, though neither is named here; 1069 names them.

1069.reading: The poet, born in a womb, beautiful in youth, babbling the learned books while his black hair turns white without understanding, asks to be taught the true knowledge that the pure, undying Vedic brahmins praise, who plunge into the fire rite twice a day and once more and bathe in water. The praise, sharing its close with 1068, tells how the demons took the crown of Amaravati, seized Indra of the thousand eyes with his elephant Airavata, ruined the land of the wish-granting tree and imprisoned the gods, whom Murugan freed.
1069.nuance: கலைநூல் பிதற்றி: book learning is mere prattle while the hair greys. The knowledge sought (இயல் போதகம்) is the one the fire-tending brahmins praise, so the song sets learning against teaching rather than rite against devotion. A corrupt glyph sits in the line about the crown, and how முருகாய் மனக்கவலையோஆட divides is unclear.

1070.reading: The poet asks whether he will end the bewilderment of carrying this pot of the senses and swarming in distress without telling, with love, of how Murugan once went to the millet field of the hunter girl who guarded it and rejoiced upon her young breasts. The praise recalls Rama, who brought the monkey hordes and ground Lanka and its demons to dust, and names Murugan lord of the gods, praised by devotees in the bliss beyond birth and death and by the three worlds.
1070.nuance: The plea is not to escape Valli's story but to sing it: telling of Murugan's love for her (நின் திறம் புகலாது) is the cure for the confusion of the senses (இந்த்ரிய கடம், the body as a pot). The middle of the praise, with the angry cloud-hued one, the three-eyed one and a fierce elephant, is hard to divide.

1071.reading: The poet calls himself one with no love that melts the heart, no nobility, character or shame, nothing to be saved by, and asks whether he will end as a quarrelsome scoundrel who speaks insolently in anger, without clearly knowing with love how Murugan went to embrace the breasts of the girl of the bowmen's hill. The praise recalls the one who arrogantly lifted the hill where Siva stays and had his heads cut off, and names Murugan, whose feet the gods of the eight directions, the sun and Indra serve, praised by the three worlds.
1071.nuance: The self-abuse is specific: not lust but anger and insolent speech (சினத்தில் மண்டி மிண்டு உரைக்கும் வம்பன்). The one who lifted Siva's hill is Ravana; who cut his heads (Rama, as in 1070) and how that clause joins the praise of Murugan is unclear.

1072.reading: The poet asks not to rejoice as if they were permanent in the house he lives in, his prattling children, kin, home town, wives, youth, wealth, wide lands and hills, but to be granted to worship Murugan with a shining lamp. The praise names him nephew of the cloud-hued one who climbed the kurundu tree, bridegroom of the hunter girl of the monkey-haunted hill, the scholar who knows the Veda and cool Tamil, and the lord of red feet and anklets.
1072.nuance: The remedy for clinging is a concrete rite, worship with a lamp (விளங்கு தீபம் கொண்டு உனை வழிபட). Murugan as the scholar of both Veda and Tamil (வேதம் தண்டமிழ் தெரிதரு புலவோன்) sets the two side by side.

1073.reading: Trusting that the wife he joined and the sons who delight his eyes would never fail him, the poet took his pleasure in the world and fell into misery, with a wasting body and grief in his heart; he asks instead for Murugan's beloved feet and the grace to speak of him. The praise names him nephew of Hari who joined the lady of the blossoming flower, bridegroom of the hunters' creeper-like girl, and lord of red feet whose anklets and bells ring in every direction.
1073.nuance: Companion to 1072: the same closing line, and the same turn from family to the feet, here as the disappointment of trust (கலங்கிடார் என்று, 'they will not falter') rather than a list of things that pass.

1074.reading: Most of the song is praise of Siva, who wears the bull, the elephant-skin cloak, ash, the sacred thread, tiger skin, axe and deer, swaying ear-ring and garland of skulls on his crown, and of Murugan as the guru whom that Lord lovingly approached, who in anger uprooted Sura with his kin. The plea asks that when the poet is spent, so that Death's messengers with their noose and rope do not torment him, Murugan come on the great peacock to end his sorrow.
1074.nuance: ஈசன் பரிவுடன் மேவிய குருநாதா: the long list of Siva's emblems builds up to Murugan as Siva's own teacher, the teaching of Om though the syllable is not named here. The plea is only two lines, for the hour of death.

1075.reading: Praising Murugan as the life of Siva who burned the three cities in an instant, the rider who drives the peacock to terrify the asuras, the six-faced lord whose vel pierced the great mountain, and the younger one who comes after the elephant-faced, big-bellied god, the singer asks whether Kama's arrows may strike the young girl who lies pale with longing. The praise ends with Murugan who embraced the hunters' daughter, nephew of Hari asleep on the serpent, lord of the whole earth who ends the deeds of devotees and the sorrows of the gods.
1075.nuance: An akam plea in the voice of someone who speaks for a lovesick girl, a mother or a friend, set inside a frame of praise; the poet's own confession is absent. பசலையொடு அணையும் is the classical pallor of love-sickness.

1076.reading: The poet describes the common women whose Meru-like breasts are adorned with civet, agil, sandal, pearls and gem chains, with lovely blue-lily eyes and nectar speech, in whose beds he melts under their sway in helpless passion, and asks Murugan to rule him, his slave who is perishing. The praise names Murugan nephew of the cloud-hued one who gathered the frightened cows with his flute and who drove the churning of the roaring sea while the mountain whirled, and lord of the one on the bee-haunted lotus.
1076.nuance: பொதுவின் மடமாதர்: women common to all, but neither money nor deceit is named, so the song stays with passion. The praise joins Krishna's flute and the churning of the ocean as feats of Vishnu, sung in drum syllables (குமுகுமு, நெறுநெறு, மொகுமொகு). The last epithet makes Murugan lord of Brahma.

1077.reading: The poet speaks of women with moon faces and eyes that rival their ear-rings, who ensnare the first understanding, and of the karma of plunging into union with them that he, a dog, has drawn on himself; he asks for the love that praises with joy the feet that give wisdom and the higher state, so that the sorrows of his mind wither. The praise names Murugan the chest where the hunter girl's breasts rest, the one who crushed the asuras and freed the gods, the beautiful Kumara who drank the milk of the six mothers, son of Uma, and lord of Hari, Hara and Brahma.
1077.nuance: வழிவழி அடிமை, hereditary service, appears in the plea, but whether the poet asks for that knowledge to widen or is complaining that it has been driven out is unclear from the split. அரி அர பிரமர் தம்பிரானே puts Murugan above the three gods.

1078.reading: Not wishing to stay in this hut of a body that comes with cruel diseases, hiccups and vomiting, bent and dulled, the poet says he has escaped from the other faiths that will crumble and come to Murugan, and asks him to set his feet on his head in a little friendship and rule him, so that he gains the true thing. The praise shows Siva, the ancient one, dancing in the bare burning ground with demons clapping and dancing round to the drum's beat and his chaste consort matching him, and names Murugan his Kumara, companion of the hunters' parrot.
1078.nuance: பரசமயத்துத் தப்பிப் போந்தேன்: the poet speaks as a convert from other sects. அடி ... தலைமேலே ... பூண்டு: the feet set on the head, the Saiva image of the guru's initiation. பதிவ்ரதை ஒத்த names Uma as the chaste wife who keeps time with Siva's dance.

1079.reading: In this world circled by the sun, wound round by the two kinds of deeds and worn out, the poet sees how the stinking body is treated: kin say 'take it quickly', drop their attachment, go to the burning ground and lay it in the fire by rule; he asks whether Murugan will not burn away this bundle of peril and rule him. The praise, paired with 1078, shows the Bhairavas, the damaru's sound and the serpent as Siva dances in the high burning ground while the tall one keeps time with his hands, and names Murugan his son, companion of the hunters' parrot.
1079.nuance: The plea turns the cremation fire into a figure for grace: kin burn the body by rule, and the poet asks Murugan to burn (காய்ந்து) the bundle of his troubles. Whether உறவோரும் means kin or is a variant of துறவோரும் (renouncers) changes the scene, and தத்துக் கத்தை is obscure.

1080.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come and rule him, removing the sorrow of his mind with release and making him know song. The praise names him the one who keeps in mind the love of the hunter girl with pot-like breasts and cuckoo speech, younger brother of the elephant born of the great god of the northern mountain, and the victor in battle who rose from the Saravana pool.
1080.nuance: A short song where praise outweighs plea. இசை அறிவித்து may mean 'teach me music' or 'make known (your) glory'; how இடமுடன் வைத்த சிந்தை divides is unclear.

1081.reading: Before he weakens, having eaten the spittle of women, thrown away the capital in his hand, whirled toward another birth, and still dared to make love when his body was withered and aching, the poet asks Murugan to rule him. The praise names him nephew of the green cloud who chose the hooded serpent as his bed, the one who spoke Tamil into the ear of the pot-born sage, and Kumara trusted by the hunter girl.
1081.nuance: கையில் முதலைக் களைந்து: the money lost is the capital itself, not just income. குடமுனி கற்க அன்று தமிழ் செவியிற் பகர்ந்த: Murugan as the teacher of Tamil to Agastya.

links.note: Tirumular says Nandi set his holy feet on his head and so drained the path to the womb; 1078 asks Murugan to set his feet on the poet's head in friendship, the same act of the guru's grace.
Both songs give the kin's words at death, 'take it quickly' (கடுகென எடும், எடும் எடு), and the body laid in the fire at the burning ground.

source_issues: 1069: corrupt glyph in வழ஧முடி (flagged by CORRUPT_CHARS).
Across the chapter a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ யிர்போமுன், உ யர்கால், உ ழல், உ சந்த, உ கந்த); read as one word.
1072: புலவோனெ for புலவோனே; 1075: வருவொனே for வருவோனே.
1077: கொண்முவா is probably கொள் மூவா; the line is unclear.
